text: The scenario follow-up calls Alfred's first planning step the "qualification" of his goals. It almost certainly means quantification: putting numbers on each goal.
Self-test answer 14 calls diet, exercise and check-ups "risk reduction". Page 2•22 and answer 13 classify them as loss prevention.
The text calls long-term disability low frequency and high severity, but the summary table on the same page files disability under high frequency and high severity (use a combination of methods).
The self-test answer key matches "risk" with "the chance of loss", but the chapter says risk is uncertainty concerning loss and is not the same as the chance of loss. Go with the chapter.
The text gives both 1993 and 1994 for when Lloyd's began admitting corporate members. 1993 is the year of the vote.
"Some of the cost borne by the insurer" in the co-insurance discussion is a typo for "insured": co-insurance makes the insured share the cost.
Commission is defined as stating an incorrect fact and omission as failing to reveal one, yet the text then calls an intentional failure to disclose "commission". Learn the clean definitions.
The self-test answer key words indemnity oddly. The principle is simpler: insurance restores you after a loss and never pays more than the loss.
Self-test answer keys 7 (waiver of premium) and 9 (endorsements) disagree with the chapter text. Go with the chapter.
The tax summary table can be read as making group health benefits taxable in Quebec. The main text (5•13) says only employer-paid health premiums are taxable in Quebec; the benefits are tax-free.
Chapter 5 says CPP/QPP contributions run from age 18 to 65, but chapter 6 (6•13–6•14) says contributions can continue up to age 70.
Chapter 5 says the $2,500 CPP/QPP death benefit goes to the estate or the surviving spouse as designated; chapter 6 (6•18) says the estate, or in Quebec whoever paid the funeral, or the heirs.
The Workers' Compensation example states a $568.80 benefit, but its own arithmetic ([$800 − $120 − $40 − $13] × 0.9) gives $564.30.
Self-test answer 2 says employers pay at least 50% of health premiums; the main text on 5•6 says disability premiums. Go with the main text.
Self-test answer 15 says Maury gets 79% of his pension, but 42 months early × 0.6% is a 25.2% cut, which leaves 74.8%.
Angela's early-pension example says 48 months × 0.6% is "28%". It is 28.8%, which matches the $252 reduction shown.
Pages 6•13 and 6•20 quote different OAS and GIS maximums because they come from different quarters of 2019. Know how the benefits work rather than one quarter's amounts.
A bullet gives the maximum defined benefit pension as $2,944.44 "in 2019", but Table 6.1 shows that is the 2018 figure; 2019 is $3,025.56 ($27,230 ÷ 9).
The ideal IPP client is aged 40 to 71 earning over $151,278 on 6•33, but age 50+ earning about $150,000 on 6•34.
The one-line RRSP room rule can be read two ways. The worked example caps 18% of earned income at the dollar limit first, then subtracts the pension adjustment.
The cost-of-waiting example says the early saver ends with about $90,000 more, but its own balances give about $83,700. The "almost 25% more" holds.
In the $500-a-year savings table, the row labelled 15 years matches 20 years of saving.
The Lifelong Learning Plan income formula prints a minus sign where a division belongs.
The under-71 RRIF minimum is printed "(1/90 – age of annuitant)". It means 1 ÷ (90 − age at the start of the year).
Appendix A lists 7.08% for both age 81 and age 82. The age-82 factor is wrong; don't memorise it.
Self-test answer 6 says a LIF can roll to a surviving spouse "under the age of 70", which clashes with the chapter's age-71 rules.

The spouse's preferential share in the chapter text (Alberta $40,000, BC $65,000, territories $50,000, Manitoba greater of $50,000 or half) disagrees with Appendix A (8•17–8•19). Expect exam questions on the principle, not these amounts.
Appendix A's Alberta row contains a stray paragraph that repeats British Columbia's "$150,000, remainder split equally" wording.
"In Quebec, a legacy to the spouse of a legatee is valid" is ambiguous; it probably means the spouse of a witness. Don't lean on this sentence.
The answer key for self-test question 15 (9•42) gives "intestate", but its own explanation and page 9•17 say the will stays valid. Go with the text.
The Quebec per capita example ("the two living children and all the great-grandchildren") is garbled. Learn the rule, not that example.
"A trust company cannot be a mandator to the person" should read mandatary: a trust company cannot act as mandatary for personal care.
Self-test question 6's Quebec answer letter does not match the option it describes. Go with the chapter text.
Manitoba's probate fee on a $1M estate is $5,995 in the text's example but $7,000 in the fee table and the self-test answer.
Page 10•18 says co-owners can dispose of their interests on their own, but 10•22 says jointly owned real estate needs every joint tenant's permission even to sell one's own share.

The end of community of property as Quebec's default regime is given as January 1, 1970 here but "married before July 1, 1970" on 11•11. July 1, 1970 is the cut-off the chapter uses for which couples fall under it.
